# What’s in a standard cup (250 mL)

Before Chapter 1 talks about plants and processing, and before Chapter 2 talks about how you *feel*, it helps to know what “a cup” even means. People say the phrase casually. Labs and home kitchens mean very different strengths.

This page standardizes on a **250 mL** cup and lists typical lab and consumer-brew ranges from the source packs. Use it as a **map**, not a promise about your exact mug. When a module mentions “200 mg L-theanine,” come back here and compare: that lab capsule is often much stronger than one ordinary mug.

## Why the numbers move

Leaf quality, brand, and steep time move the numbers. Green and black tea also differ because of processing (see [Chapter 1](modules/module-01.qmd)): many catechins stay simple in green tea; in black tea many are linked into darker pigments, so EGCG and total catechins in the cup are usually much lower.

The table uses a common everyday baseline: **2 g dry leaf per 250 mL** (one bag or a modest spoonful). Formal tasting (ISO 3103) uses about **2 g per 100 mL** (about **5 g per 250 mL**)—stronger than many home cups.

If your green tea tastes mild, you may be below these ranges. If your black tea keeps you up, you may be toward the high end of caffeine (about **40–80 mg** in these sources for the black-tea row). Compare cups using the same volume when you can.

## Typical yields (packs)

| Compound | Tea type | Typical yield | Usual brew in these sources | Citation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Caffeine | Green | **30–50 mg** | 2 g leaf, 250 mL, 80°C, 3 min | Chin et al. (2008) |
| Caffeine | Black | **40–80 mg** | 2 g leaf, 250 mL, 100°C, 3–5 min | Hicks et al. (1996) |
| L-Theanine | Green | **15–30 mg** (shaded Gyokuro or Matcha often **45–80 mg**) | 2 g, 250 mL, 80°C, 3 min | Keenan et al. (2011) |
| L-Theanine | Black | **10–25 mg** | 2 g, 250 mL, 100°C, 3–5 min | Keenan et al. (2011) |
| EGCG | Green | **50–120 mg** | 2 g, 250 mL, 80°C, 3 min | Perva-Uzunalić et al. (2006) |
| EGCG | Black | **1–10 mg** (most converted during oxidation) | 2 g, 250 mL, 100°C, 3–5 min | Del Rio et al. (2004) |
| Total catechins | Green | **100–300 mg** | 2 g, 250 mL, 80°C, 3 min | Bhagwat et al. (2011) |
| Total catechins | Black | **10–50 mg** (many linked into darker pigments) | 2 g, 250 mL, 100°C, 5 min | Lakenbrink et al. (2000) |

## Practical notes (still from the packs)

**Water temperature.** Hotter water pulls more catechins. Steeping green tea at **100°C** instead of **80°C** can raise total catechin yield by about **25%**, but it also pulls more bitter material and can hurt taste. That is the same brew-temperature thread Chapter 1 uses when it talks about EGCG needing heat.

**Why 250 mL?** Papers often use 200 mL or 250 mL. This site standardizes on **250 mL** so comparisons stay consistent.

**Leaf amount.** Formal tasting (ISO 3103) uses about **2 g per 100 mL** (about **5 g per 250 mL**). The table above uses a common everyday baseline: **2 g dry leaf per 250 mL** cup (one bag or modest spoonful).

**Beginner tip.** When you read Chapter 2 study doses like “200 mg L-theanine,” compare them to this table: a typical green cup here is about **15–30 mg** L-theanine (shaded Gyokuro or Matcha often **45–80 mg**). Lab capsules are often much stronger than one ordinary mug.

From here, the natural next stop is [Chapter 1](modules/module-01.qmd)—how those numbers got into the water in the first place.
